title: Estimating, costing, and valuation
summary: Three related but distinct activities, and most questions turn on keeping them apart: estimating predicts the cost of work not yet done, costing builds up the rate for a unit of work, and valuation determines the present worth of property that already exists. The other half of the subchapter is IS 1200 — the measurement conventions that decide what a contractor is actually paid. Learn the units and the two deduction thresholds (0.1 m² for brickwork, 0.5 m² for plaster) exactly, and learn the estimate types by when in the project each is prepared.

sections.heading: Types of estimate and when each is prepared
sections.body:
The estimate types make sense only in **sequence**, because each is prepared with the information available at that moment.

| Estimate | Prepared | Basis |
|---|---|---|
| **Preliminary / approximate** | At **conception**, for administrative approval | **Plinth area rate**, cube rate, or per unit |
| **Plinth area** | Early | Plinth area × rate from a similar completed building |
| **Cube rate** | Early | Plinth area × height × rate |
| **Approximate quantity** | Early | Rough quantities of the **main items** only — the most accurate of the approximate methods |
| **Detailed** | Before **calling tenders** | **Item by item**, measured and rated |
| **Revised** | During execution, when cost exceeds sanction by **> 5%** | A fresh detailed estimate |
| **Supplementary** | During execution, when **more work** is needed | Detailed, for the **added items** only |
| **Annual repair / maintenance** | Yearly | Upkeep |
| **Complete** | — | Including land, legal, supervision — the **whole** project cost |

**Why an approximate estimate comes first.** At conception the design does not yet exist. A detailed estimate needs **complete drawings**, which cannot be produced until the project is approved and funded — so an approximate figure must come first, sufficient for the authority to decide whether to proceed.

The project sequence: **approximate estimate → administrative approval → detailed design → detailed estimate → technical sanction → expenditure sanction → tender and award → execution → completion report and final bill.**

**Administrative approval** sanctions the *proposal*. **Technical sanction** is the engineer's own responsibility: it certifies that the quantities, specifications and rates are correct, and is granted by an officer competent for that value of work. Signing a technical sanction for an estimate one has not checked is precisely the casual certification that professional conduct rules exist to prevent.

**Revised or supplementary?** The single discriminating question is **whether the scope has changed**:

| | **Revised** | **Supplementary** |
|---|---|---|
| Covers | **The same work**, re-costed | **Additional work** |
| Trigger | Sanctioned amount exceeded by **> 5%** | New work is needed |
| Presented | A **complete fresh estimate** with a **comparative statement** item by item | An estimate for the **added items only**, with the original attached |
| Answers | *Why does the same work now cost more?* | *What is this new work and what does it cost?* |

The **comparative statement** is what a revised estimate must carry — original quantity and rate against the new, with a reason for each variation. Without it the authority cannot tell an honest cost increase from an admission of poor estimating.

A supplementary estimate must be **sanctioned before the work is done**. Executing unsanctioned work commits public money without authority, and if sanction is later refused the expenditure is irregular and the engineer personally answerable. The same applies to **variation orders**: issued **in writing and in advance**, valued at contract rates where the work is of the same character. There is a second reason for the advance order — additional work justifies an **extension of time**, and without the written order there is no basis for it, leaving the contractor exposed to liquidated damages for a delay the employer caused.

**A caution against habitual supplementary estimates.** They are legitimate for genuinely unforeseen needs, but a project repeatedly requiring them usually had an inadequate **investigation and design** stage. The remedy is better preliminary work, not smoother paperwork.

sections.heading: Approximate estimating and the areas
sections.body:
> **Approximate cost = plinth area × plinth area rate**

The rate is drawn from a **recently completed building of similar type, specification and locality**, and the whole validity of the estimate rests on that similarity. The same plinth area of a warehouse, a school and a hospital cost very different amounts, because the rate silently carries the specification — finishes, services, structural system.

| Method | Basis | Suits |
|---|---|---|
| **Plinth area rate** | Plinth area × rate/m² | **Buildings** — the standard method |
| **Cube rate** | Plinth area × **height** × rate/m³ | Buildings of **unusual storey height** |
| **Unit rate (service unit)** | Cost **per unit of function** | **Per bed** (hospital), per student, per seat, **per km** (road), per litre (reservoir) |
| **Bay method** | Cost of one repeating **bay** × number of bays | Factories, workshops, long sheds |

The **cube rate** exists because cost follows **volume** more closely than floor area once storey heights depart from normal: a 6 m hall costs far more per square metre than a 3 m office, since walls, columns and services all scale with height.

The **unit rate** method is how public infrastructure is budgeted at policy level — a road at so much per kilometre, a school per classroom. Crude, but it is the only method available before any design exists, and it works because **function determines most of the cost**.

**The three areas**, in descending order of size:

| Area | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Plinth (built-up) area** | Area at floor level measured **externally**, over the plinth — **everything**, walls included |
| **Carpet area** | The **usable** floor area |
| Super built-up area | A **marketing** figure — plinth plus a share of common areas; not a technical term |

> **Plinth area = carpet area + area of walls + circulation and service areas**

**Excluded from carpet area**, each for a reason: **walls** (not usable), **verandahs, staircases, corridors, lift wells** (circulation), **sanitary accommodation**, shafts and ducts.

> **Carpet area ≈ 50 – 70% of plinth area** for a residential building

Walls alone account for **10–15%**, circulation the rest. A claimed carpet area above about 75% of plinth area should be questioned.

**Which area is used for what:** **plinth area** for estimating and for municipal **floor area ratio** and building permission; **carpet area** for **rent and sale**, because it is what the occupier actually gets. An engineer asked to certify areas must state **which** area is being certified.

**Plinth area measurement rules:** measured **external** to the walls at floor level; **courtyards, open verandahs and open balconies excluded**; covered verandahs included; and areas of **different storey height or specification measured separately**, because each attracts its own rate.

**Accuracy must be stated.** An approximate estimate is reliable to about **±10 to 15%** when based on a genuinely comparable building, and worse when it is not. Quoting one to the nearest rupee with no stated tolerance invites it to be treated as a commitment — and many cost overruns begin as an approximate estimate that was never described as approximate.

sections.heading: Detailed estimating — the two methods and the provisions
sections.body:
**Centre line method:**

> **Quantity = total centre line length × breadth × depth**

One length serves **every** item of a wall — excavation, foundation concrete, footings, superstructure masonry — which makes it quick and internally consistent.

**Its essential correction**, and the reason candidates lose the mark: at every **junction** of walls the method **over-measures**, because both intersecting walls claim the shared corner.

> **Deduct half the breadth of the item, for each junction, per cross wall**

A T-junction needs one deduction, a cross-junction two. A rectangular building with **no internal walls** needs **no** correction, since its centre line is a closed loop.

**Long wall–short wall method:** **long walls measured out-to-out** (centre to centre plus the two half-breadths), **short walls in-to-in** between them — so each corner belongs to the long walls only, once each. It is therefore **self-correcting**.

| | **Centre line** | **Long wall–short wall** |
|---|---|---|
| Speed | **Faster** | Slower |
| Junctions | Need **deduction** | **Automatic** |
| Suits | Walls of **uniform thickness** | Walls of **differing thickness**, complex plans |
| Risk | Forgetting the junction deduction | Arithmetic slips over many items |

The long wall–short wall method is preferred where thicknesses change between footing, plinth and superstructure — because a change of thickness changes the out-to-out and in-to-in lengths but **not** the centre line, which is exactly when the centre line method's simplicity becomes a liability.

**Order of items** in a building estimate, since the same lengths are reused: earthwork excavation → lime/cement concrete in foundation → footings and foundation masonry → DPC → superstructure masonry → RCC → doors and windows → flooring → roofing → plastering → finishing → services.

**The percentage provisions**, commonly examined together:

| Provision | Typical rate | For |
|---|---|---|
| **Contingencies** | **3 – 5%** | Minor **unforeseen** items |
| **Work-charged establishment** | **1.5 – 2%** | Site staff engaged **for that work** |
| Tools and plant | 1 – 1.5% | Departmental tools |
| Petty supervision | 1.5 – 2% | — |
| **Contractor's profit** (in **rate analysis**) | **10 – 15%** | The contractor's margin |
| Water charges | 1 – 2% | — |

The trap is offering **10–15%** as a contingency figure: that is the **contractor's profit** within *rate analysis*, a different provision at a different stage.

**What contingency is NOT for:** design changes (a **supplementary** estimate), a large rate increase (a **revised** estimate), items **omitted by oversight**, or **price escalation** (a separate clause). It is deliberately small because it is meant only for genuinely minor items.

**Why accuracy matters beyond arithmetic.** The estimate is the basis on which work is **sanctioned**, on which **funds are allotted**, and against which tenders are judged. An estimate materially below the true cost stalls the work halfway for want of funds; one materially above locks up money that could have been spent elsewhere. Both are professional failures.

sections.heading: Measurement — IS 1200
sections.body:
**The organising principle**, worth more than the individual entries:

> **The unit of measurement follows the dimension that actually governs the cost.**

| If cost varies with | Unit | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **All three dimensions** | **m³** | Concrete, brickwork, earthwork, stone masonry |
| **Area**, thickness specified | **m²** | **DPC**, plastering, flooring, painting, **half-brick walls** |
| **Length**, section specified | **running metre** | Skirting, dado, cornice, railing, kerb, pipes |
| **The mass of material** | **quintal / tonne** | **Reinforcement**, structural steel |
| Nothing but the count | **number** | Sanitary fittings, manholes, trees |

So **DPC in m²** and **brickwork in m³** is not arbitrary: a DPC's thickness is fixed by the drawing, while a wall's varies with the item. A **half-brick wall** goes in m² for the same reason.

**Steel by weight**, because that is how it is bought and because bars of equal length differ enormously in value by diameter:

> **Unit weight = d²/162 kg per metre**, d in mm

From (πd²/4) × 7850 ÷ 10⁶. Check: 12 mm → 144/162 = **0.888 kg/m**; 16 mm → **1.58**; 20 mm → **2.47**. **Laps, hooks and bends are included** in the measured length; binding wire and spacers are not.

**The two deduction thresholds**, constantly interchanged:

| Work | No deduction for an opening up to |
|---|---|
| **Brickwork and masonry** | **0.1 m²** |
| **Plastering** | **0.5 m²** |

**Why plastering's is larger** — and this reasoning is worth more than the numbers. A small opening in a plastered wall saves a trivial area of plaster but **costs extra labour**: the plasterer must work around the reveal, form neat edges and finish the corners. The two roughly cancel, so small openings are ignored. Brickwork has no comparable edge-labour penalty, so its threshold is much lower.

**Plastering deductions in detail:**

| Case | Rule |
|---|---|
| Up to **0.5 m²** | **No deduction**; no addition for reveals either |
| **0.5 to 3 m²** | Deduct on **one face only**; no addition for reveals |
| **Over 3 m²** | Deduct on **both faces**; reveals, jambs and soffits **added** |

The middle row shows the scheme's neatness: for a medium opening the one-face deduction and the omitted reveals roughly offset, keeping the arithmetic simple while the cost stays fair.

**Painting** has a parallel device: a panelled door is measured as its **plain area × a multiplying factor** (about 1.3 per side), rather than on its developed surface — easier to measure and more honest about the labour.

**Earthwork** is measured in **m³ on the authorised dimensions shown on the drawing, not as actually excavated.** A contractor who digs wider than specified is not paid for the extra — the risk of over-excavation lies with the contractor, which is why side slopes and trench widths in the drawings matter commercially as well as technically.

**Lead and lift**, the paired earthwork terms: **lead** is the **horizontal** distance the material is carried, **lift** the **vertical** height it is raised. Both affect the rate. An **initial lead (commonly 30 m)** and **initial lift (1.5 m)** are included in the basic rate, with extra paid in stages beyond. For a deep pit the **lift** dominates the cost; for a road project the **lead** does.

**Three volumes for the same soil** — confusing them is the most consequential error in earthwork estimating:

| Volume | Where | Relation |
|---|---|---|
| **Bank (in situ)** | Undisturbed | The base |
| **Loose** | In the truck | **Larger** — bulked 20–30% |
| **Compacted** | In the embankment | **Smaller** than bank by 10–20% |

So 100 m³ excavated may yield 125 m³ to haul and only about 90 m³ of embankment: **the quantity to excavate is not the quantity to fill.**

**General rules:** linear dimensions to **0.01 m**, areas to 0.01 m², volumes to 0.01 m³; work of **different specifications measured separately**; work in **different situations** (below ground, above 3 m height) measured separately; and all measurements recorded in the **measurement book (MB)** — page-numbered, in ink, corrections initialled and never erased, signed by both the measuring officer and the contractor. The MB is the document on which every running bill is paid and the primary evidence in a dispute.

**Why this matters commercially.** In an **item-rate contract** the contractor is paid **measured quantity × tendered rate**, so IS 1200 is the arbiter of payment. Site disputes concern **how a quantity was arrived at** far more often than the rate agreed — because the rate is in the contract while the measurement is made afterwards.

sections.heading: Rate analysis and specifications
sections.body:
**Rate analysis** builds up the rate for a unit of finished work — per m³ of concrete, per m² of plaster — from its constituents:

1. **Materials** — quantity per unit, at current market rates, plus wastage
2. **Labour** — the number of each class of worker per unit, at scheduled wages
3. **Plant and machinery** — hire or depreciation charges
4. **Overheads** — usually a percentage (water, supervision, establishment)
5. **Contractor's profit** — commonly **10–15%**

The sum is the rate entered in the bill of quantities. **Task work (out-turn)** figures give the labour component — the quantity a given class of worker completes in a day.

**Distinguish the four neighbours carefully**, since each is a separate examination item:

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Rate analysis** | Working out the **rate per unit of an item of work** |
| **Detailed estimate** | Quantities of every item × their rates = the total project cost |
| **Valuation** | Determining the **present worth of an existing property** |
| **Specification** | A written description of the **materials, workmanship and quality** required — it fixes *how*, not *how much* |

**Specifications** come in two kinds. **General specifications** describe the class of work briefly, for the client's understanding. **Detailed specifications** describe each item's materials, proportions, workmanship, method, tolerances and tests, and form part of the contract. Their purpose is to make the drawing's silence unambiguous: a drawing shows dimensions, a specification shows quality. Where the two conflict, the contract states which prevails.

In Nepal, rate analysis draws on the **District Rate** published annually for each district and on the government **Norms** for material and labour coefficients, which is why the same item legitimately carries different rates in different districts.

sections.heading: Valuation and depreciation
sections.body:
**Valuation** determines the **present worth** of property that already exists — the reverse direction from estimating.

**Methods, by what the property is:**

| Method | Basis | Suits |
|---|---|---|
| **Rental (capitalised value)** | **Net income × year's purchase** | Income-producing property |
| **Cost / depreciation** | **Replacement cost less depreciation**, plus land | Owner-occupied buildings, insurance |
| **Comparative (market)** | Recent sales of **similar** property | An active market |
| **Development** | Value after development, less cost to develop | Land ripe for development |
| **Profit-based** | Capitalised trading profit | Hotels, cinemas, business premises |

**The rental method's arithmetic:**

> **Net income = gross rent − outgoings**
> **Year's purchase (YP) = 100 / rate of interest**
> **Capitalised value = net income × YP**

Outgoings: **repairs ≈ 1/12 (8⅓%) of gross rent**, municipal taxes, insurance, management and collection, a **sinking fund** for eventual rebuilding, and an allowance for **voids**. The sinking fund entry is the one candidates omit — since the building has a finite life, part of the income must be set aside to replace it, and only the remainder is true return on capital.

**Note the inverse relation**, which is the substance of the concept:

| Expected return | YP | Value |
|---|---|---|
| **5%** | **20** | **Higher** |
| 8% | 12.5 | — |
| **10%** | **10** | **Lower** |

A **higher** required return gives a **lower** valuation for the same income. That is not an accounting artefact but an economic truth: an investor demanding more return will pay less. The rate chosen therefore reflects the **risk** of the income — a secure, well-let building is capitalised at a low rate and valued highly. **Choosing the rate is the valuer's central judgement**, and it moves the answer more than any other input.

For a **limited-term** lease rather than a perpetuity, YP is the present value of an annuity, **[1 − (1+i)^−n]/i**, sometimes at a **dual rate**.

**Depreciation methods:**

| Method | Annual charge | Pattern |
|---|---|---|
| **Straight line** | **(C − S)/n** | **Uniform** |
| **Sinking fund** | (C − S) × **i/[(1+i)ⁿ − 1]** | Uniform, but **credits interest** |
| **Declining balance** | Fixed **% of reducing book value** | **Accelerated**; never reaches zero |
| Sum-of-years-digits | (remaining life / Σ years) × (C − S) | Accelerated |
| **Production units** | Per **unit of output** | Follows **use** |

Straight line: **book value = C − m(C − S)/n**, falling linearly from C to S. Worked example: a mixer at Rs 500,000 with Rs 50,000 salvage over 10 years depreciates **Rs 45,000/year**, giving a book value of Rs 320,000 after 4 years.

The **sinking fund** method recognises that money set aside **earns interest**, so the annual deposit is less than a simple division. For Rs 100,000 over 10 years at 8%: 100,000 × 0.069 = **Rs 6,900/year**, against Rs 10,000 straight line. The accumulated interest supplies the difference.

**Depreciation is not merely bookkeeping.** It determines the **hire or ownership rate** charged for plant, and hence the rate analysis for every item that plant performs. It also feeds **replacement analysis**: keep or replace is decided by comparing the **equivalent uniform annual cost** of the old machine — which **rises** as maintenance grows and remaining value falls — against that of a new one. The **economic life** is where the two cross.

**The valuation terms**, routinely confused:

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Book value** | Cost **less accumulated depreciation** — an accounting figure, unrelated to any market |
| **Salvage value** | Worth at end of life, sold **intact and working** |
| **Scrap value** | Worth of the **dismantled materials** — about **10% of cost** for a building, **net of demolition** |
| **Market value** | What a willing buyer would pay **today** |
| **Replacement value** | Cost of an **equivalent new** asset at current rates |
| Sentimental / distress value | Above or below market, for non-economic reasons |

The **salvage/scrap** distinction is whether the asset survives as a **working thing** or only as **material**. Scrap value can be **negative** where demolition, disposal and site restoration cost more than the materials fetch — quite common for reinforced concrete.

Book value and market value can diverge sharply: a fully depreciated machine with a book value of zero may still command a substantial price. An engineer asked for "the value" must establish **which** value is wanted before answering.

And throughout: **land does not depreciate.** It is valued separately and added, which is why the worth of an old property in a good location is often almost entirely its land.

formulas.label: Approximate cost (plinth area method)
formulas.expression: Cost = plinth area × plinth area rate (from a similar completed building)
formulas.note: Accuracy about ±10–15% when genuinely comparable. Cube rate = plinth area × height × rate.

formulas.label: Centre line method
formulas.expression: Quantity = total centre line length × breadth × depth,   less ½ breadth per junction per cross wall
formulas.note: No correction needed for a rectangular building with no internal walls.

formulas.label: Unit weight of a round bar
formulas.expression: w = d² / 162 kg per metre   (d in mm)

formulas.label: IS 1200 deduction thresholds
formulas.expression: Brickwork: no deduction up to 0.1 m².   Plastering: no deduction up to 0.5 m².
formulas.note: Plastering's is larger because the extra edge labour offsets the area saved.

formulas.label: Capitalised value
formulas.expression: Capitalised value = net annual income × YP,   where YP = 100 / rate of interest
formulas.note: A higher required return gives a LOWER valuation. At 8%, YP = 12.5.

formulas.label: Straight line depreciation
formulas.expression: D = (C − S) / n;   book value after m years = C − m(C − S)/n
formulas.note: Falls linearly from C to S. Salvage value S, not zero.

formulas.label: Sinking fund depreciation
formulas.note: Less than straight line, because the fund earns interest. The factor is the sinking fund factor (A/F).

formulas.label: Volume relations in earthwork
formulas.expression: loose = bank × (1 + bulking);   compacted = bank × (1 − shrinkage)
formulas.note: Bulking 20–30%, shrinkage 10–20%. The quantity to excavate is NOT the quantity to fill.
